## The core difference

Both take work from two branches and combine it. They differ in what they do to history.

**Merge** creates a new commit with two parents. Your branch's commits stay exactly as they are — same SHAs, same timestamps, same parent pointers. The merge commit is the join point.

```
main    A---B---C-------M
                 \     /
feature           D---E
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of a new base. `D` and `E` are not moved — they're *re-created* as `D'` and `E'` with different SHAs, different parents, and (usually) different content, since each is re-applied as a diff against a new context.

```
main    A---B---C---D'---E'
```

The mental model that matters: merge is **additive and non-destructive**; rebase **rewrites**. A rebased commit is a different commit that happens to look similar.

## Consequences that actually bite

**Conflicts.** Merge resolves conflicts once, in one commit. Rebase resolves them potentially once *per commit* being replayed — you fix the same conflict in `D`, then again in `E`. For a long branch against a drifted base, this is genuinely painful. (`git rerere` helps; so does rebasing often rather than once at the end.)

**Intermediate commits get silently broken.** Rebase replays each commit and stops only on conflicts, not on test failures. A commit can apply cleanly and still not build, because it was written against a world that no longer exists. Your final state is fine, your `git bisect` history is not. If you care, `git rebase -x 'make test'` runs a command after each replayed commit.

**Shared branches.** Rebasing commits others have pulled forces them into recovery — their old commits and your new ones both exist, and a naive `git pull` merges the two copies together, duplicating everything. This is the real reason for the "golden rule": *don't rebase public history*. It's not aesthetic; it's that you can't rewrite something other people already have.

**Force-push risk.** Rebase implies `git push --force`. Always use `--force-with-lease` — it refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched, which catches the case where a colleague pushed to your branch. Plain `--force` will happily discard their work.

## When to reach for each

**Rebase** when the branch is yours alone and hasn't been shared, when you're pulling in upstream changes mid-development (`git pull --rebase` avoids a merge commit for every sync), or when you're cleaning up before review — squashing "fix typo" and "actually fix typo" into something a reviewer can read. `git rebase -i` is the tool for that last one, and it's the strongest argument for rebase: reviewers read commits, and rebase is how you make them readable.

**Merge** when the branch is shared, when the branch point is information you want to keep (long-lived release branches, anything you might need to reason about later), and — this one is underrated — when the branch is long and the base has drifted a lot. The one-shot conflict resolution is worth more than the linear history.

**Merging a finished feature into main** is a separate decision from *how you kept the branch current*. The common good setup: rebase locally to keep your branch tidy, then merge into main with `--no-ff` so the feature remains a visible, revertable unit. `git revert -m 1 <merge>` undoes an entire feature in one command; undoing a squashed or fast-forwarded range is fiddlier.

## The practical default

Rebase your own in-flight work; merge anything shared or anything whose branch structure is worth preserving. If you're on a team, this is usually a settled convention rather than a per-PR choice — check what your repo does before changing it, since mixed conventions produce the worst history of all.

Two safety notes: `git rebase --abort` gets you out of any rebase cleanly, and `git reflog` recovers commits you rewrote away — rebase is scary but rarely actually destroys anything within the ~90-day reflog window.
